To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the duration of a compressive force on a rat nerve root is a key determinant of the magnitude of the force required to maintain that force; and (2) the duration of the compressive force on the rat nerve root is correlated to the duration of behavioral hypersensitivity and astrocyte activation.

(1) the biomechanical properties of the nerve root are time-dependent, (2) the time-dependent properties correlate with the degree of glial activation in the spinal cord, and (3) the time-dependent biomechanical properties and glial activation correlate with behavioral sensitivity to pain.
the duration of nerve root compression is an important determinant of behavioral and spinal glial responses in a rat model of nerve root compression.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the time-dependent properties that underlie the pathophysiology of nerve root compression, and may help to identify the critical time frame during which a nerve root is susceptible to damage.
the time-dependent properties that may influence pain-related behavioral and spinal glial outcomes.
understanding the mechanisms underlying pain and glial activation following a nerve root compression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
compression durations of 30 seconds, 3 minutes, or 15 minutes induce significant biomechanical and physiologic changes in the nerve root and spinal cord, respectively.
the time-dependent mechanical properties of the nerve root are related to the duration of the compression and to the pain and glial activation.
the biomechanical and behavioral results of this study indicate that a sustained compression of 15 min is necessary for a significant increase in behavioral sensitivity and spinal glial activation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the time-dependent properties in the mechanical response of the nerve root under compression correlate with the time-dependent properties for the behavioral and physiological responses in the nerve root compression model of radicuopathy.
compression duration is critical in the context of behavioral sensitivity and spinal glial activation.
compression of the nerve root induces pain symptoms and spinal gliosis.
The main takeaway from our work is that

compression of the rat C6-C8 root in situ for durations ranging from 30 seconds to 15 minutes can be used to model radiculopathy, and that the duration of compression is an important factor in determining the degree of behavioral hypersensitivity and the degree of glial reactivity that develops in the dorsal horn.
the duration of compression may be a critical factor in the development of pain symptoms following nerve root injury.

compression of the nerve root for durations of 3 min or greater can lead to sustained behavioral hypersensitivity and increased activation of astrocytes and microglia in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, and these changes may be mediated, in part, by a reduction in the mechanical properties of the root.
